text: Socrates does not start his city from an idea. He builds it out of need, in Book II of the Republic, on the ground that no one is self-sufficient (369b). The first citizens are a farmer, a builder, a weaver, and a shoemaker, and each does the one work his nature suits (370a–c). A city that stayed at that size would never need a soldier. Glaucon refuses to live there and calls it a "city of pigs." He wants couches and side dishes, and Socrates grants him a "feverish" city of luxury (372d–e). In the feverish city appetite grows, and the growth ends in war. The land that fed the healthy city cannot feed the feverish one, so the city must take a slice of its neighbors' land and defend its own (373d–e). A class of warriors follows of necessity, and with it comes the question that occupies the rest of the reading: what kind of person can be trusted with weapons? Socrates answers with a well-bred dog, gentle to those it knows and fierce to strangers (375a–e). From the dog he draws the first of the city's many surprises. The dog, and the guardian modeled on it, tells friend from enemy by knowledge, and anything that does so is "a lover of learning" (376b). The guardian is already a philosopher of a kind.
